title: Neuroscience, Wellbeing, and Urban Design: Our Universal Attraction to Vitality
research_question: This review article aims to synthesize findings from neuroscience, psychology, and urban planning to argue that human beings have a deep, intrinsic affinity for vitality in built and natural environments, and that designing urban spaces to capture this 'life-stuff' is key to promoting psychological wellbeing and creating psychologically sustainable cities.

participants.description: Not applicable, as this is a review article synthesizing existing literature. The author briefly describes participants in their own pilot studies but does not provide detailed demographics or N for those specific studies within this paper.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Pairs of images (e.g., different styles of nature, buildings) used in informal investigations to assess perceived 'life'.

A chain-link fence with public art (laser-cut plywood panels depicting local environment features) vs. a simple chain-link fence with advertisements, used as experimental and control sites in Toronto, Canada, to study pedestrian behavior.
Public squares rendered in virtual reality, with classical vs. modernist designs, presented to either the central or peripheral visual field in an immersive slide show.
Point light displays (PLDs) showing biological motion; animated displays of small numbers of geometric shapes moving in coordinated patterns (Heider and Simmel experiment).

Chimeric stimuli consisting of images of natural settings presented to one part of the visual field (center or periphery) and images of built settings presented to the other part of the field, shown very briefly (66.6 milliseconds).

measures.instrument: Self-report (indicating which image contains more life)

findings.antecedent: Built spaces imbued with Alexander's 15 fundamental properties
findings.consequent: Perceived 'life' in built spaces and promotion of wellbeing
findings.mechanism: These properties convey liveliness, which is key to establishing design principles that promote wellbeing.
findings.quote: Alexander sets out to reach the foundation of the phenomenon of life in the built environment. Arriving at a set of 15 fun-damental properties that he says imbue built spaces with life, he argues that these properties, and the liveliness that they convey, are the key to establishing design principles that promote wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: Evidence of vitality in natural and built settings
findings.consequent: Human mind's innate receptivity and positive response
findings.mechanism: The human mind is innately receptive to evidence of vitality and, in most cases, responds positively to such evidence.
findings.quote: my argument that the human mind is innately receptive to evidence of vitality and, in most cases, responds positively to such evidence in natural and built settings.

findings.mechanism: Humans are predisposed to sometimes perceive non-face objects as if they are faces, possibly due to specialized face processing modules in the brain (FFA).
findings.quote: In a strange phenomenon called pareidolia, we seem to be predisposed to sometimes perceive non-face objects-even buildings-as if they are faces

findings.antecedent: Point light displays (PLDs) of biological figures
findings.consequent: Accurate assessment of actor's gender and mood
findings.mechanism: Humans are exquisitely sensitive to the motion parameters of PLDs, processed by specialized brain areas like the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and mirror neurons.
findings.quote: most humans are exquisitely sensitive to the motion parameters of PLDs and can use them to accu-rately assess the gender and mood of actors

findings.antecedent: Seemingly random patterns of motion of geometric shapes
findings.consequent: Interpretation of objects as animate characters with goals, motivations, and emotions
findings.mechanism: The human brain is predisposed to find life and imposes such properties on random non-biological patterns, reflecting an innate tendency to process motion by imposing a narrative structure.
findings.quote: we have an innate tendency to process the motion of inanimate objects by imposing a narrative structure upon it.

findings.antecedent: Public art fence (designed façade depicting local environment features)
findings.mechanism: Subtle interventions in the urban landscape can have a robust impact on human behavior, leading pedestrians to slow down and engage more with the environment.
findings.quote: At the public art site, pedestrians initially walked at around the same speed but eventually slowed to speeds that were sometimes only half of the average walking speed at the control site

findings.consequent: Pedestrian pausing and head turns towards the fence
findings.mechanism: The artistic design captures attention and encourages engagement, leading to more exploratory behavior.
findings.quote: pedestrians paused more often in front of the public art fence and turned their heads toward it significantly more often

findings.mechanism: Low complexity fails to engage curiosity, leading to lower positive affect and arousal, consistent with Berlyne's theory that too little stimulation is negative.
findings.quote: participants reported low levels of positive affect in settings that were rated as low in complexity. Not only this, but when we monitored autonomic arousal... we found a relationship between façade complexity and physiological arousal. Overall, our results demonstrated that low-complexity settings produced a combination of low positive affect and low arousal.

findings.antecedent: View of nature from hospital room
findings.consequent: Pain levels and recovery periods for patients
findings.mechanism: Natural environments contain features that lower stress (SRT) or elicit soft fascination, regenerating selective attention (ART).
findings.quote: observed lower levels of pain and shorter periods of recovery for patients who resided in rooms that had a view of nature rather than those that faced a blank wall.

findings.antecedent: Images containing fractal dimensions (approx. 1.4-1.5) common in natural scenes
findings.mechanism: The inherent power of self-similarity, a low-level visual property, influences both aesthetic preference and physiological state, acting as a 'signature' for nature.
findings.quote: images containing fractal dimensions seen most commonly in natural scenes (those with fractal dimensions of approximately 1.4-1.5), are those that elicit the strongest positive affective re-sponses.

findings.antecedent: Visual information contained within certain spatial frequencies (in images, natural or not)
findings.consequent: Differentiation between images with and without restorative potential, and influence on aesthetic preference and eye movement
findings.mechanism: Spatial frequency preference is a well-characterized property of visual perception areas in the brain, aligning with scene processing mechanisms.
findings.quote: only visual information contained within certain spatial frequencies will differen-tiate between images that either do or do not have restorative potential... and yet they influenced aesthetic preference and eye movement.

findings.antecedent: Scenes presented only to the peripheral visual field (even briefly, 50ms)
findings.consequent: Accurate processing of scene gist and elicitation of affective responses
findings.mechanism: The coarse processing of the peripheral visual field is sufficient to drive human preference for vitality, suggesting rapid ambient visual processing.
findings.quote: participants who are presented with scenes for a very brief duration, even when restricted to the peripheral field, are capable of accurately processing the gist of a scene... scenes presented only in the periphery were able to elicit affective responses. This suggests that the coarse processing of the peripheral visual field is sufficient to drive the human preference for vitality.

findings.antecedent: Classical urban designs (containing more features present in natural settings) presented to peripheral visual field
findings.mechanism: Classical designs, with their greater 'vitality' features, elicit more positive affective responses even when processed peripherally, supporting the idea of an intrinsic human response to vitality.
findings.quote: some preliminary indication that classical designs were associated with more positive affect than the modern designs, even when presented only to the peripheral visual field.

findings.antecedent: Brief peripheral presentation of an image
findings.consequent: Bias toward stimuli that show vitality (preference)
findings.mechanism: Rapid, peripheral processing is sufficient to drive preferences for vitality, suggesting a fundamental, low-level mechanism.
findings.quote: this recently completed work suggests that such brief peripheral presentation of an image can elicit preferences that suggest a bias toward stimuli that show vitality.

findings.antecedent: Urban designs that take advantage of intrinsic human responses to vitality
findings.consequent: Positive affective states in exposed individuals
findings.mechanism: Harnessing the intrinsic human response to vitality, which is rooted in our biology, leads to improved psychological wellbeing.
findings.quote: When urban designs take advantage of these intrinsic responses, they are more likely to engender positive affective states in those who are exposed to them.

mechanisms: Innate human affinity for vitality, possibly rooted in biology and evolutionary lineage.
Specialized brain modules for face perception (FFA) and biological motion (STS, mirror neurons).
Human predisposition to impose narrative structure and 'life' on inanimate patterns.
Curiosity as a powerful driver of behavior, heightened physiological arousal (Berlyne's theory).
Stress reduction (SRT) and attention restoration (ART) mechanisms in response to natural settings.
Low-level visual properties like fractal dimensions (1.4-1.5) and specific spatial frequencies as 'signatures' for nature and vitality.
Ambient visual processing in the peripheral field for rapid gist perception and affective responses, guiding subsequent focal vision.
Bottom-up processing of environmental features influencing affective and physiological states.
moderators: Environmental complexity (curvilinear relationship, though inverted-U is debated).
Type of visual field presentation (central vs. peripheral).
implementation_implications: Urban design should incorporate features that promote vitality to improve psychological wellbeing and create psychologically sustainable cities.
Design principles should be based on accumulated knowledge of sensory systems, neuroscience, and cognitive science.
Harnessing the intrinsic human response to vitality can positively change behavior and improve psychological wellbeing.
Increasing importance should be placed on design features that improve urban mood and remove barriers to social cohesion, reducing urban loneliness and suffering.
Good design for human environments, at any scale, should capture 'life-stuff' and might emerge from bottom-up, local urban planning practices.

tables.description: A pair of images of different styles of nature. Which one has more life?
Image of a building illustrating pareidolia.
Photographs of the designed fence (upper) and control fence (lower) used in the study of the influence of façade design on pedestrian behaviour.
A bar graph showing mean walking speed as a function of time of day, segment, and façade design. The graph shows that pedestrians slowed down during the walk along the designed fence.

View of the modern glass plaza, looking back toward a classical facade, in one of the immersive VR environments created for the study of central and peripheral vision. The chrome egg was included as a feature of interest to aid in legibility

limitations: Alexander's work has detractors due to reliance on intuition rather than careful experiments, rather than the conduct of careful experiments.
The contrasting effects of classical and modern design in the VR study were subtle, indicating preliminary findings.
The mechanism through which natural scenes exert their restorative effect remains unclear, despite clear evidence for the effect.
The pilot field study on façades did not control for subtle differences in intentions between pedestrians walking in different directions.
The paper acknowledges that the inverted-U function for complexity might be an oversimplification and neglects other factors.
The distinction between 'where and how' and 'what' visual pathways should not be overstated due to necessary communication and cooperation between them.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Although urban planners and architects have understood that there is a relationship between the design of a setting and our thoughts and emotions, it is only recently that we have had the tools to properly dissect this relationship. New methods for measuring brain states in field settings in immersive virtual reality have generated a host of novel findings, but a theme that connects many of these findings together is the idea that human beings have a deep affinity for vitality at every level from the interior of a home to an urban streetscape. Not only this, but recent evidence suggests that we respond to the vitality of scenes almost immediately, even after exposures as brief as 50 milliseconds, possibly using ambient visual processing mechanisms that rely on our peripheral visual field. Further, when we sense and respond to vitality, positive affect increases, which in turn promotes affiliation and buffers us against urban loneliness. I will present findings from experiments both in the laboratory and in the field that show the power of vitality to effect behavioural change, and I will argue that harnessing this power is one of the keys to building a psychologically sustainable city.
